LESSONS.title: Reading and writing JSON
LESSONS.goal: Convert JSON with json.loads and json.dumps
summary: JSON is data shaped as a string
json.loads: string → dictionary
json.dumps: dictionary → string
JSON null is None; check it with if

cards.say: Web APIs send data as a string in a shape called JSON. From the outside it looks a lot like a dictionary. json.loads turns that string into a real dictionary.
cards.code:
import json
raw = input()
data = json.loads(raw)
print(data["menu"], data["won"] + 500)

cards.say: The other way around, json.dumps turns a dictionary into a JSON string. To keep letters like ê as they are, pass ensure_ascii=False. Without it, they turn into the \uXXXX shape.
cards.code:
import json
d = {"menu": "crêpe", "won": 4500}
s = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False)
print(s)

cards.say: JSON's null becomes Python's None after loads. It means “no value”, so you can check whether it's empty with if not. You'll meet it a lot when there's no next page.
cards.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"next": null}')
print(d["next"])
if not d["next"]:
    print("Last page")

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"n": "5"}')
print(d["n"] + "1")
items.explain: In JSON, "5" wrapped in quotes is a string. + between strings joins them, so you get 51.

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"open": false}')
print(d["open"])
items.explain: JSON's true, false and null become Python's True, False and None after loads. The first letter is uppercase.

items.code:
import json
d = {"b": 1, "a": 2}
s = json.dumps(d, sort_keys=True)
print(s)
items.explain: sort_keys=True lines the keys up in name order. So a comes before b, and the quotes are double quotes.

items.q: Fill in the blank so 4500 is printed.
items.code:
import json
raw = '{"menu": "tea", "won": 4500}'
d = json.loads(raw)
print(d[___])
items.explain: The key name is "won", wrapped in quotes. "price" is a key that doesn't exist, so KeyError, and won without quotes isn't the name of anything, so NameError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so Done comes after 700.
items.explain: You have to import json first to use loads. Then loads makes a dictionary, and you take out the value and print it.

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"next": "p2"}')
if not d["next"]:
    print("Done")
print("More")
items.explain: "p2" has a value, so not d["next"] is false. “Done” is skipped and only “More” is printed. If it were null, both would come out.

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"prev": null}')
print(d["prev"])
items.explain: JSON's null becomes Python's None after loads. No quotes, and not lowercase null either.

items.task: Read one line of JSON with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and store it in data with json.loads. It has menu and won. Print the price for the next size up (won + 500) in the form “latte 5000 won”. Example: {"menu": "latte", "won": 4500} gives latte 5000 won
hints: The menu name and price change with the JSON you get as input. The keys may come in a different order, too.
json.loads, which you just learned, turns a JSON string into a dictionary.
Store the result of loads in data, take out menu and won by key name, and add 500 to won.

import json
data = json.loads(input())
won = data["won"] + ___
(print menu and won on one line)
items.solution:
import json
data = json.loads(input())
won = data["won"] + 500
print(data["menu"], str(won) + " won")
items.explain: You take values out by key name, so it works even when the JSON keys come in a different order. The edge case of won being 0 also comes out right as 500 won.

items.q: What does JSON's true become after loads?
items.explain: true becomes Python's boolean True. It's not the string "true" but a real boolean, so you can use it in an if right away.

LESSONS.title: Nested structures
LESSONS.goal: Take things out of a list inside a dictionary, one layer at a time
summary: Chain brackets to go down one layer at a time
Lists use numbers, dictionaries use keys
Loop over the orders in a list with for

cards.say: JSON can hold more JSON inside it, like a list in a dictionary or a dictionary in a list. To take values out, chain brackets and go down one layer at a time.
When dictionaries line up, like in an order list, take them out one by one with for. Each time around, o is one order, and you read it by key, like o["item"].
cards.code:
import json
data = json.loads(input())
for o in data["orders"]:
    print(o["item"], o["qty"])

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"a": [10, 20, 30]}')
print(d["a"][1])
items.explain: d["a"] is the list [10, 20, 30], and its index 1 is 20. Indexes count from 0.

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"u": {"age": 20}}')
print(d["u"]["age"] + 1)
items.explain: d["u"] is another dictionary, so ["age"] goes down one more layer. 20 plus 1 is 21.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"u": {"age": 20}}')
print(d["age"])
items.explain: age is inside u, so it isn't a key of the outer d, and you get a KeyError clue. Go down one layer at a time with d["u"]["age"].

items.q: Fill in the blank so the total 12 is printed.
items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"p": [3, 4, 5]}')
total = 0
for n in d[___]:
    total += n
print(total)
items.explain: The list to loop over is under the key "p". The other keys don't exist, so they give a KeyError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so latte, tea and Done come out in turn.
items.explain: After loads, for takes out the orders one at a time and prints them. The last line has no indentation, so it runs only once, after the loop ends.

items.task: Store the JSON from input() (leave the parentheses empty) in data with json.loads. Multiply price by qty for each order in the orders list, add them all up with for, and print “Total: N won”. Example: two 4500-won drinks and one 3000-won drink give Total: 12000 won
hints: You need the total no matter how many orders there are. What's the total when there are no orders at all?
Think back to the running total in Chapter 5. Start at total = 0 and add for each order.
Loop over data["orders"] from loads with for, and for each order add price times qty to total.

import json
data = json.loads(input())
total = 0
for o in data["orders"]:
    total += o["price"] * ___
print(f"Total: {total} won")
items.solution:
import json
data = json.loads(input())
total = 0
for o in data["orders"]:
    total += o["price"] * o["qty"]
print(f"Total: {total} won")
items.explain: Starting total at 0 means you get 0 won even with no orders. Adding price * qty one order at a time keeps the flow clean.

options: The first order in the orders list
items.explain: data["orders"] is a list, and [0] is its first slot, the first order. From that order (a dictionary) you then take out "qty".

LESSONS.title: Calling an API
LESSONS.goal: Send a request to a practice API and read its JSON response
summary: urlopen → read → decode → loads
The body is bytes, so it needs decode
A missing address raises HTTPError

cards.say: An API is an address that programs call. Read the body with read, turn it into a string with decode, then loads it, and you get a dictionary. Real code sends the request to an API on the internet, but here a practice server answers.
cards.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/bus/101"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["route"], data["min"])

cards.say: APIs can fail too. A stop that doesn't exist is a 404, so you get an HTTPError. Wrap it in try from Chapter 10 and you can show a friendly message instead of a clue.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
url = "https://ria.example/bus/999"
try:
    res = urlopen(url)
except HTTPError:
    print("No such stop")

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/bus/202"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["route"])
items.explain: You took the route key from the response for stop 202. The response looks like {"route": "Bus 14", "min": 9}.

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/bus/303"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["route"], data["min"])
items.explain: Give print two values with a comma and they go on one line with a space between. 0 minutes means it's arriving now.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/bus/999"
res = urlopen(url)
print("Got it")
items.explain: For status codes of 400 and up, like 404, urlopen tells you with an HTTPError. The error stops the code before it reaches print.

items.q: Fill in the blank to turn the response into a string.
items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/bus/1"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().___("utf-8")
print(json.loads(text)["route"])
items.explain: The body that read gives back is bytes. decode("utf-8") turns it into a string you can print and work with. (loads can actually read bytes too, but here we turn it into a string first.)

items.q: Fill in the blank to turn the string into a dictionary.
items.code:
import json
text = '{"route": "Bus 7", "min": 4}'
data = json.___(text)
print(data["min"])
items.explain: loads is the one that turns a string into a dictionary. dumps goes the other way, so the result is still a string, and ["min"] on a string is a TypeError. json has no decode.

items.task: Read a stop number with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and store it in stop. Add stop to the end of "https://ria.example/bus/", request it with urlopen, and print route and min, read with json.loads, in the form “Bus 7 in 4 min”. 101 gives Bus 7 in 4 min
items.starter:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
hints: The end of the address changes with the number you enter. What address do you get if you enter 202?
An address is a string, so you can join it with +. Read the response in the order urlopen, read, decode, loads.
Request the url with stop added to the end, then take route and min out of the dictionary you get by loads-ing the body.

base = "https://ria.example/bus/"
stop = input()
url = base + ___
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
(print route and min here)
items.solution:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
base = "https://ria.example/bus/"
stop = input()
url = base + stop
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
route = data["route"]
mins = data["min"]
print(f"{route} in {mins} min")
items.explain: You built the address from the input, so it can call any stop. The edge case of 0 minutes comes out fine too.

items.q: What's the right order to turn the response body into a dictionary?
items.explain: Read the bytes (read), turn them into a string (decode), and make a dictionary (loads). Change the order, and a step won't have the result it needs from the step before.

LESSONS.title: Building a query string
LESSONS.goal: Call an API with parameters added by urlencode
summary: After the address: ?name=value&name=value
urlencode joins a dictionary for you
The dictionary's order is the query's order

cards.say: The ?name=value part after an address is called a query string. Instead of joining it yourself, give urlencode a dictionary and it builds it for you. A space becomes +, and letters like é turn into safe % codes.
cards.code:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
p = {"stop": 101, "line": 7}
print(urlencode(p))
print(urlencode({"q": "café latte"}))

cards.say: Request with address + ? + query string. Same API, but change just the parameters and you get a different response. Here we ask about bus 7 at stop 101.
cards.code:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
p = {"stop": 101, "line": 7}
qs = urlencode(p)
url = "https://ria.example/bus?" + qs
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
print(json.loads(text)["min"])

items.explain: urlencode joins name=value pairs with &. It doesn't add the ? at the front, so you put it in yourself when joining it to the address.

items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
print(urlencode({"q": "café latte"}))
items.explain: Spaces and letters like é can't go into an address as they are, so the space becomes + and é becomes % with hex digits. The server on the other end reads them back as é and a space.
urlencode joins things in the order you put them in the dictionary. If the server cares about order, write the dictionary in that order too.

items.q: Fill in the blank so stop=101 is printed.
items.code:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
qs = ___({"stop": 101})
print(qs)
items.explain: Joining a dictionary into name=value is urlencode's job. json.dumps prints a JSON string shaped like {"stop": 101}, and json.loads can't read a dictionary, so TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the full address is printed.
items.explain: Import urlencode, make the query string qs, then join it to the address. qs has to exist before url can use it.

items.task: Read a stop number and then a line with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and store them in stop and line. urlencode a dictionary in the order stop, line, add it after "https://ria.example/bus?", request it with urlopen, and print route and min read with json.loads. 101 and 7 give Bus 7 4
items.starter:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
hints: The two inputs become the two values in the query. What comes after the address if you enter 202 and 14?
urlencode, which you just learned, makes the stop=…&line=… shape from a dictionary.
Turn {"stop": stop, "line": line} into a query with urlencode, add it to the address, and read it like in 14-3 to take out route and min.

p = {"stop": stop, "line": ___}
qs = urlencode(p)
url = "https://ria.example/bus?" + qs
(then urlopen, read, decode, loads, print)
items.solution:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
stop = input()
line = input()
p = {"stop": stop, "line": line}
qs = urlencode(p)
url = "https://ria.example/bus?" + qs
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["route"], data["min"])
items.explain: You put the inputs in a dictionary and built the address with urlencode. Any stop and line work with the same code, and 0 minutes is exact too.

options: Joins a dictionary into name=value pairs
Sends a request to an address
items.explain: urlencode doesn't send a request. It only builds the query string. urlopen sends requests, and loads reads JSON.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 14 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Call an API, read its JSON and summarize it
summary: loads/dumps go between JSON and dictionaries
Chain brackets to go down nested structures
urlencode → urlopen → loads, in that order

cards.say: Let's wrap up Chapter 14. Build an address with a query string, send the request, turn the JSON into a dictionary, and take values out of the nested structure. That flow is the basics of web APIs.
cards.code:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
qs = urlencode({"c": "seoul"})
url = "https://ria.example/w?" + qs
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
t = data["today"]
print(data["city"], t["temp"])

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads('{"n": 2.5}')
print(d["n"] * 2)
items.explain: 2.5 in JSON is a number (a float), so after loads you can multiply it. A value without quotes isn't a string.

items.code:
import json
d = json.loads(input())
print(d["w"][1]["t"])
items.explain: d["w"] is a list, and index 1 is the second dictionary, {"t": 8}. Take "t" from it and you get 8.

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/w?c=busan"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["today"]["sky"])
items.explain: You took sky from inside today. Busan's today is {"temp": 21, "sky": "cloudy"}.

items.q: Fill in the blank so c=jeju is printed.
items.explain: urlencode needs a dictionary. "params" in quotes is a string, so TypeError, and jeju without quotes is a NameError.

items.code:
import json
d = {"b": 1, "a": 2}
s = json.dumps(d, indent=2)
print(s)
items.explain: indent=2 breaks lines and indents by two spaces to make it easy to read. There's no sort_keys, so the keys stay in the order you put them: b, a.

items.task: Read a city code (like seoul) with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and store it in c. Build the address "https://ria.example/w?" + a query made with urlencode, request it with urlopen, then json.loads the response. Print “Seoul sunny 18C” on the first line and, on the second line, “Weekly high 21C”, found by looping over week with for.
items.starter:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
hints: Every city gives a different response. Some cities have weekly temperatures below zero, and one has only one day.
Think back to the Chapter 14 flow: urlencode for the address, urlopen for the request, loads for the dictionary.
The first line is city plus today's sky and temp. For the second line, set best to the first temp in week and change it whenever a bigger value comes along.
items.solution:
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import urlopen
c = input()
qs = urlencode({"c": c})
url = "https://ria.example/w?" + qs
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
today = data["today"]
city = data["city"]
sky = today["sky"]
temp = today["temp"]
print(city, sky, str(temp) + "C")
best = data["week"][0]["temp"]
for d in data["week"]:
    if d["temp"] > best:
        best = d["temp"]
print(f"Weekly high {best}C")
items.explain: You start the highest temperature from the first value, not from 0, so freezing Chuncheon comes out right too. One-day Jeju is no problem, and the request-and-read flow is clean.

items.q: What does the query string after ? in an address look like?
items.explain: Like ?c=seoul&n=2, it joins name=value pairs with &. That's how you tell the server your conditions and get the response you want.

ADVANCED.title: Collecting paged results
ADVANCED.goal: Follow next and collect every page's items into one list
summary: Lots of data comes split into pages
When next is null, it's the last page
Collect each page's items into one list

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. APIs split lots of data into pages. The null you saw in 14-1 sits in "next" on the last page.
cards.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/shop"
url = root + "?page=1"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
n = len(data["items"])
print(n, data["next"])

cards.say: Follow the page numbers until next becomes None. Take out each page's items and collect them in names, and stop at the last page with if not data["next"]:.
cards.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/shop"
names = []
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "?page=" + str(page)
    res = urlopen(url)
    text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
    data = json.loads(text)
    for it in data["items"]:
        names.append(it["name"])
    if not data["next"]:
        break
    page = data["next"]
print(len(names), names[-1])

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/cafe"
url = root + "?page=2"
res = urlopen(url)
text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["next"])
items.explain: Page 2 of cafe is the last one, so it has "next": null. After loads, null becomes None, so None is printed.

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/cafe"
total = 0
page = 1
while True:

items.code:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/snack"
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "?page=" + str(page)
    res = urlopen(url)

items.q: Fill in the blank so all pages are collected and 3 is printed.

import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
root = "https://ria.example/cafe"
names = []
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "?page=" + str(page)
    res = urlopen(url)

import json
a = json.loads('{"items": [1, 2]}')

all_items = a["items"] + b["items"]

items.task: Read a store name (one of shop, cafe, snack) with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Starting at ria.example/<store>?page=1, follow next until it's null, add up won for all items, and print the count and total. Example: snack gives Items: 1, total: 1800 won
items.starter:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
kind = input()
root = "https://ria.example/" + kind
hints: Each store has a different number of pages. Start at page 1 and keep going to the last page (next is null).
Inside while True, send the request, loop over each page's items adding them up, and break if it's the last page.
Set the count and total variables to 0 before the loop. Change the page number with data["next"].

count = 0
total = 0
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "?page=" + str(page)
    (read and loads → add up each page)
    if not ___:
        break
items.solution:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
kind = input()
root = "https://ria.example/" + kind
count = 0
total = 0
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "?page=" + str(page)
    res = urlopen(url)
    text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
    data = json.loads(text)
    for it in data["items"]:
        count = count + 1
        total = total + it["won"]
    if not data["next"]:
        break
    page = data["next"]
msg = f"Items: {count}, total:"
print(msg, str(total) + " won")
items.explain: Even without knowing the number of pages ahead of time, you stop at the page whose next is None, so one-page snack and three-page shop both come out right. You add on every page, so all the items get in.

items.q: What tells the page-following loop when to stop?
options: next on the last page is null
items.explain: The API sends "next": null on the last page. In Python that's None, so if not data["next"]: catches it.

ADVANCED.title: Saving JSON to a file
ADVANCED.goal: Write to a file with json.dump and check it by reading with json.load
summary: json.dump(data, f) writes to a file
json.load(f) reads from a file
In this app, files vanish when the run ends

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. json.dump(data, f) writes JSON to a file, and json.load(f) reads from a file. In this app, files vanish when the run ends.
cards.code:
import json
d = {"menu": "latte", "won": 4500}
with open("a.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(d, f)
with open("a.json") as f:
    back = json.load(f)
print(back["menu"], back["won"])

cards.say: ensure_ascii=False keeps letters like ê as they are, indent=2 breaks lines, and sort_keys=True puts keys in name order. A list you built with append can be dumped whole, too.
cards.code:
import json
rows = []
a = {"won": 4500, "menu": "crêpe"}
b = {"won": 3800, "menu": "chai"}
rows.append(a)
rows.append(b)
with open("m.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(
        rows, f,
        ensure_ascii=False,
        indent=2, sort_keys=True,
    )
with open("m.json") as f:
    print(f.read())

items.code:
import json
with open("n.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"n": 5}, f)
with open("n.json") as f:

import json
n = int(input())
rows = []
for i in range(n):
    parts = input().split()
    row = {"menu": parts[0]}
    row["won"] = int(parts[1])
    rows.append(row)
with open("menu.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(
        rows, f,
        ensure_ascii=False,
        indent=2, sort_keys=True,
    )
with open("menu.json") as f:
    back = json.load(f)
total = 0
for r in back:
    total = total + r["won"]
msg = f"Items: {len(back)}, total:"
print(msg, str(total) + " won")

items.solution:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen
city = input()
site = "https://ria.example/w?c="
root = site + city
temps = []
page = 1
while True:
    url = root + "&page=" + str(page)
    res = urlopen(url)
    text = res.read().decode("utf-8")
    data = json.loads(text)
    for d in data["days"]:
        temps.append(d["temp"])
    if not data["next"]:
        break
    page = data["next"]
total = sum(temps)
avg = round(total / len(temps), 1)
rep = {
    "city": city, "avg": avg,
    "max": max(temps),
    "min": min(temps),
}
with open("report.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(
        rep, f,
        ensure_ascii=False,
        indent=2, sort_keys=True,
    )
with open("report.json") as f:
    back = json.load(f)
print(back["city"])
print("Average", back["avg"])
print("High", back["max"])
print("Low", back["min"])
items.explain: Thanks to next, both one-page jeju and two-page seoul stop at the right place. max and min compare freezing temperatures (-5) and 0 by size, and round keeps the average to one place, like -2.3.

options: Rounds to the nearest value at one decimal place
items.explain: round(x, 1) keeps one decimal place and rounds to the nearest value, so 3.666… becomes 3.7. That's different from rounding down to an integer or chopping off digits.
